COLUMN: The oil market sees the future of the US-Iran war as binary. Either they reach a deal — in days — or they head into war again, perhaps as soon as early November. There is, however, a third path: The current deadlock becomes the new normal.  https://t.co/hGsUpfQ3CW

The North Sea market continues to benefit from expensive freight, inflating the cost of Dated Brent versus other physical grades. Notable: CPC, the flagship export grade from Kazakhstan, was offered today at a record discount of almost -$10 a barrel to Brent.

Saudi Arabia has been exporting crude so far this month at a rate that suggests the kingdom has lifted its oil production toward the 9-10 million b/d range.

Using both the Persian Gulf and (more importantly) the Red Sea, Riyadh has boosted crude exports during the first 22 days of October to >7 million b/d, reaching pre-war levels (see @Vortexa chart below). Adding clean and dirty refined product, the export flow Oct 1-22 reaches ~8.5m b/d, slightly below pre-war levels of >9m b/d. 

The crude export surge -- and the production boost -- could be part of a "use-while-you-can" strategy aimed at pumping ahead of the potential restart of the war post US midterms (or before the Houthis of Yemen damage another key oil installation -- several near misses already in recent days, including an attack that killed two contractors near a major oilfield).

Note: using Oct 1-2 as typically it takes at least five days for dark transits across the SoH to become clear.

#Commodities - European morning comment

#CrudeOil trades higher amid reports of renewed US warnings of military strikes that could derail tentative diplomatic efforts that calmed the market on Tuesday. With uncertainty surrounding the Israeli election and the US midterms just days away, the risk of renewed escalation remains elevated. Ultimately, both Washington and Tehran need to agree on the way forward and that road remains elusive for now, and until credible signs of de-escalation emerge, the market is likely to remain highly sensitive to geopolitical headlines, with a substantial risk premium embedded in prices. Focus on EIA's weekly report, Israeli election, and FOMC.

#Gold trades lower after an Asia rebound to USD 4070 ran out stem with rising yields and a firmer dollar ahead of today's important FOMC meeting weighing on prices. Having rebounded from key technical support around USD 3,970, the tug of war between short-term momentum sellers and longer-term accumulators continues, with bulls taking some comfort from the latest recovery and the market's ability to defend this important level. Resistance levels to watch: USD 4070 and 4230.

#Wheat: Futures extended their decline on Tuesday, with the December contract trading near a 3½-month low amid currency-related pressure and a fading Black Sea risk premium. The latest weakness followed reports that Moscow is considering proposals to secure grain shipments through the region, raising hopes of improved export flows and reduced disruption risks. December futures have fallen to around USD 6.11 per bushel, the lowest since July and down 23% from the multi-year high reached only last month.

COT report go twice-weekly from December.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission plans to double the frequency with which it publishes a widely followed report on futures and options trading positions.
The Commitment of Traders report, currently released every Friday afternoon, gives an overview of trading positions in derivatives for energy and commodities, as well as for currencies, equity indices and interest rates.
Starting in December, the CFTC will publish the report every Wednesday and Friday at 3:30 p.m. New York time, according to a Tuesday statement.
